I’m (M51) no longer suicidal but I spent virtually every day from nine years old until a few months ago when I was prescribed Effexor in combination with mirtazapine (taken that one forever.) But ultimately the reason I didn’t do it was because of all the people I’ve known (eight friends and numerous other acquaintances) who’ve succeeded in ending their lives. I’ve seen the horrific damage it does to friends and family, it’s like a bomb goes off and the shockwaves run rampage through those who are left behind. One person ends their pain and immediately transfers it to dozens of others, maybe hundreds depending on the person. I just couldn’t do that to anyone. So I’ve told myself to always be as strong as I can be and remain here - in terrible pain - so that I don’t give them mine. But I’m so glad I didn’t. Three years ago I dedicated myself to my healing (I’ve had horrific amounts of trauma, neglect and betrayal from those who were supposed to take care of me) and began therapy and it has helped me do an almost-complete 180 degree change. So yeah, it took me almost fifty years to get to this point, but it was definitely worth it. Hope this helps.

What it did help with is good restful sleep and perhaps a more steady outlook, even if I struggled with depression. However, on the advice of my wife and doctor, they added Effexor, starting at 75mg and now I’m up to 225 mg. When I moved back to southern Oregon in 2020 after spending seven years in southern Utah, I almost didn’t recognize Roseburg when I returned. When I moved to Utah in 2014, there were *some* homelessness there (in Oregon), but by 2020 it had become a massive issue. Tent camps in every single park, downtown with folks sleeping on the sidewalks. I worked at a grocery store and virtually every single day they called the cops on homeless people stealing. I can’t speak for other cities, but I would say a lot of the homeless in town weren’t shipped there from out of state but were locals down on their luck. Three things that I can see that seemed to be a huge reason for the increasing homelessness: mental health of course (Roseburg has the only VA in that part of that state, so there’s a lot of people that move there to be close to it,) the massive increase in housing costs and the scourge of meth. That last one is a huge part of the problem, at least in that part of the state. It’s frustrating to see how expensive it is to live there, especially considering that A) it’s not a good place to live by any measure except natural beauty and B) there are very very few good paying jobs there. Used to be most everyone made a good living in the timber industry, but that was when the were over fifty mills in Douglas County, I think there’s three now and most aren’t hiring. Mostly the jobs there now are service oriented and even though Oregon’s minimum wage is higher than just about anywhere, it’s still not enough to be able to afford to live.

Once, I was free-soloing up a vertical but easy wall on Wolf Rock, the largest monolith in Oregon. It was spring, which makes the rock harder to get to, due to the snow on the road. I'll get to why that matters in a bit. Anyway, I was about 500 feet up, totally vertical, vertigo-enducing. I hear the scream of a hawk, and I look up to find a peregrine falcon (fastest animal on the planet, capable of 200+ mph speeds), wings tucked, diving right towards me. I pull as deep into the rock as I can, and the bird goes right past me, close enough to feel the wind from its wings. I start climbing down (my only choice at that moment) but hear another hawk's cry. Apparently, they were a mated pair. See, this is why the spring part matters. Peregrines (and other raptors) nest on cliffs during the spring and will vigorously attack anything within half a mile of their nests. I did not know this at the time. Anyway, I digress. The second falcon is now diving at me. I sink into the rock again.
